title: Learning Heterogeneous Tactile Representation for General Dexterous Manipulation
abstract: Tactile sensing is an indispensable modality for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, a capability that hints at the ultimate frontiers of embodied intelligence. However, commercially available tactile sensors are still at a relatively early stage of development, with each type of sensor offering irreplaceable strengths alongside its own drawbacks. A key challenge is thus to free tactile understanding from sensor-specific physics, so that embodied models can effectively leverage heterogeneous tactile data. To this end, we develop LingBot-Touch, a tactile foundation model characterized by the following properties. (i) Our model yields a unified representation across different tactile sensors (i.e., piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors), and is easily extensible to new sensor types. (ii) The resulting tactile tokens are plug-and-play: they can be seamlessly integrated into policy models across paradigms, from diffusion policy to vision-language-action (VLA) models such as π_{0.5} and LingBot-VLA, consistently enhancing manipulation dexterity. (iii) Extensive experiments, spanning simulation and real-robot deployments across multiple hardware platforms, demonstrate that our tactile representation substantially benefits complex manipulation tasks while maintaining strong computational efficiency. We believe the findings in this work demonstrate the potential of leveraging cross-sensor data to scale tactile learning, and offer encouraging insights for the design of future hardware and embodied models.

title: Sage-Taiyi: A Metacognitive Architecture for Scientific Discovery
abstract: We introduce Sage-Taiyi, a metacognition-inspired architecture that uses accumulated scientific understanding to guide what to investigate next and how to investigate it. Through explicit monitoring and control, the system revises its understanding of evidence, assumptions, and unresolved questions, then uses these assessments to adapt research targets and select reusable reasoning methods. On Taiyi-Bench, an AI co-scientist ideation benchmark comprising 265 tasks from 50 papers across ten disciplines, Sage-Taiyi ranks first on all eight metrics of historical rediscovery and open-ended ideation, achieving an Overall score of 54.0 compared with 47.9 for the strongest baseline, AI Scientist-v2. It also performs well on two external scientific ideation benchmarks. Five expert-guided collaborations further connect its proposals to experimental and computational validation across chemistry, materials science, and engineering. In chemistry, reaction-condition optimization raises the yield of cobalt-catalyzed carbonylation from trace amounts to 84% and photocatalytic allylic amination from 13% to 69%. These results support metacognitive regulation as an approach to scientific ideation and its progression toward practical validation.

title: Infrathon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization
abstract: In this work, we study whether frontier agent can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from 6.82% with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to 19.86%. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, Our Infrathon framework provide resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions.

title: Reframe: Observation-Aligned Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Visual Reasoning
abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) offer complementary routes to post-training. For visual agents, however, tool use presents two related challenges. Models may overlook useful tool-returned observations, while poorly grounded actions can limit the evidence available for subsequent distillation. We introduce Reframe, a post-training framework that treats the observation state, rather than only the output distribution, as an object of alignment. First, Ground-Drop-GRPO (GD-GRPO) trains spatial and temporal specialists with evidence-aware rewards and stochastic removal of the original visual input, encouraging them to acquire grounded evidence and use the returned observations. Second, Observation-Gated-MOPD (OG-MOPD) replaces deficient tool actions with canonical ones mid-rollout and resumes distillation from the repaired observation. The two stages complement each other, as learning to rely on tool-returned observations can help the policy benefit from observation repair. Neither stage requires a task-specific SFT cold start. Extensive experiments over 14 image and video benchmarks demonstrate that Reframe outperforms both Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD. Ablation results show that GD-GRPO increases observation dependence and tool gain compared with outcome-based GRPO.

title: G-STAR: Group-Scaled Token Capacity for Deeply Compressed Autoregressive Generation
abstract: Discrete autoregressive models offer a scalable framework for image generation. However, they face a fundamental trade-off: long token sequences preserve representation quality but slow generation, while aggressive spatial compression reduces representation capacity. Based on product quantization, we show that, under a fixed nominal information budget, group size should scale quadratically with the per-axis spatial compression factor. Building on this principle, we propose GSTAR, a spatial--group co-scaling framework that enables \(32\times\) and even effective \(64\times\) compression while preserving strong reconstruction, understanding, and generation performance. Since larger groups introduce intra-group dependencies that must be modeled efficiently, we analyze their impact on inference latency and generation quality and introduce a semi-autoregressive decoder that combines parallel feature computation with lightweight causal modeling. With these designs, our highly compressed models perform competitively with leading models across five representative text-to-image benchmarks (GenEval, DPG-Bench, PRISM, LongText-Bench, and Qwen-Image-Bench). At \(1024\times1024\) resolution, our model delivers a \(20\times\) speedup over prior discrete autoregressive models, generating each image in 2.5 seconds on a single NVIDIA H200. Together, these results show that highly compressed discrete representations can enable high-quality autoregressive generation at low latency.

title: One Table, Many Queries: Benchmarking Generalist Tabular Models Across Generation, Imputation, and Prediction
abstract: Generation, imputation, and prediction query different aspects of the same tabular distribution, but are usually evaluated separately. This leaves unclear which capabilities they share, how their training objectives interact, and whether one model can perform all three well. We introduce the One Table Benchmark (), spanning 56 datasets, 46 registered methods, and 20 capability axes under aligned data splits and explicit task contracts. We compare task ranks on aligned support, train five backbones under all seven non-empty objective combinations on five datasets with three seeds, and contrast fixed-model profiles with specialist portfolios. Rank comparisons connect imputation and prediction through numerical recovery and dependence preservation, and link generation to both through predictive utility; distributional fidelity follows different, sometimes opposing, rankings. Objective interventions show the largest pooled gains from including the recipient's own objective. Generation has the broadest coverage of positive pooled auxiliary effects, while prediction shows potential to improve imputation and synthetic-data utility, with responses that vary across backbones. Cross-addition effects reveal that objective benefits need not add and depend on the objectives already present. Fixed-model comparisons expose corresponding utility--fidelity trade-offs: some generalists surpass specialist portfolios on utility, while fidelity continues to favor specialization. Frozen foundation models show strong prediction and numerical point imputation, together with promising synthetic-data utility, highlighting their potential across all three tasks. These findings motivate unified tabular models that share useful conditional information while improving categorical reconstruction and faithful joint sampling.

title: Read Less, Solve More: Token-Efficient Sparse Reading of External Content for AI Agents
abstract: Web-facing AI agents repeatedly access webpages, documents, repositories, and tool responses, yet reading interfaces often expose entire objects when only sparse evidence is needed. This over-reading increases token and latency costs and can dilute relevant evidence. We present SparseRead, a reusable reading control layer that governs content admission without modifying the agent model. Its Read Intent Protocol tracks evolving needs and source coverage; Adaptive Reader Backends select how evidence is located and exposed; and the Budgeted Read Gate bounds cumulative raw exposure per episode with faithful full-view fallback. A unified Reader interface supports interchangeable evidence acquisition across heterogeneous resources. Across six models, including Claude Opus 5, and five scenarios, SparseRead reduces total tokens by up to 92.9% and wall time by up to 89.0%, preserving or improving task quality in 97% settings. On Web deep-search tasks, it reduces tokens by 31.0--43.0% and task completion time by 23.0--37.0%. Ablations validate the three designs, while integration with three agent frameworks demonstrates portability.

title: WorldFoundry: Towards Unified Infrastructure for World Intelligence
abstract: Visual generative models increasingly blur the line between synthesizing observations and simulating environments. Yet visual plausibility alone does not constitute successful world modeling: compelling outputs may lack persistent state, physical dynamics, or causally consistent responses to interactions. We define a generative world model as a predictive dynamical system that maintains a persistent, history-conditioned representation of an environment, updates that representation in response to actions or interventions, and generates temporally coherent trajectories that reflect outcomes under observed and counterfactual interventions. From this definition, we derive an intelligence-oriented framework spanning perceptual grounding, persistent state modeling, controllable transformation, dynamics-aware prediction, and closed-loop interaction. We present WorldFoundry, open-source infrastructure for reproducible inference and evaluation across video, 3D and 4D, embodied action, and interactive world systems. WorldFoundry unifies model and benchmark discovery, runtime and asset preparation, execution orchestration, artifact management, and interactive visualization, while modality-specific adapters preserve native inputs, execution semantics, output representations, and evaluation protocols. Explicit manifests, durable artifact contracts, and evidence-aware scorecards separate execution readiness from evaluative claims, making each claim traceable to its supporting artifacts. The catalog contains 270 model entries, 74 benchmarks, and 62 registered metric entries, with readiness and execution evidence recorded separately. WorldFoundry enables reproducible comparison of persistent, controllable dynamics across heterogeneous systems, advancing the field from perceptual synthesis toward measurable world intelligence.

title: Ensemble Routing for Prompt-Adaptive Cost-Aware LLM Inference
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support Web-based services that must balance response quality and inference cost across heterogeneous requests. Conventional routing selects one model per prompt, while fixed ensembles cannot adapt their composition and cost to individual requests. We introduce PISA, a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router, and PISA-E, its extension to ensemble routing. At the core of both methods, PISA combines soft cluster memberships with model-specific predictors to estimate individual model capabilities. Building on these estimates, PISA-E jointly selects ensemble composition and cardinality under an explicit cost--quality preference that can be adjusted at inference time without retraining. A tractable ensemble-success surrogate and efficient candidate selection enable this extension without ensemble-specific training. Across four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, PISA achieves the highest macro-average cost--performance hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers in both settings. Meanwhile, PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches when prioritizing response quality, surpassing the strongest competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points under ID and OOD conditions, respectively. At selected lower-cost operating points, it also exceeds the strongest ensemble competitors' macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% and 25%, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of prompt-adaptive capability estimation for both single-model routing and selective ensembling.

title: Toward the Era of Agentic Embodied Intelligence
abstract: Foundation models increasingly guide robot actions, yet sustained autonomy requires efficient control and failure recovery. We introduce A2-MEAS, an embodied multi-agent framework built around code as a scaling interface. Learned correction codes combine corrective language, spatial evidence, execution history, and action proposals. MetaBrain provides training supervision and runtime guidance. A correction encoder and adapter absorb this knowledge into policy weights during training, while fresh codes adapt behavior with frozen weights at deployment. The action model, A2-WLA, adds motion-aware history and a latent world model to a vision-language-action policy. Surprisingly, this simple design with action pretraining and task specialization reaches 0.5755 Q-score on the 50-task BEHAVIOR 2026 public subset before online correction, 2.21x the 2025 winner's reported 0.2605 across different benchmark editions and training configurations. On all 100 BEHAVIOR 2026 public tasks, A2-MEAS achieves 0.6411 Q-score and 45.40% task success. On RoboTwin 2.0, A2-WLA achieves 93.98% average success, rising to 95.05% with the complete system. Across 12 real-robot tasks in five household settings, A2-WLA achieves 57.92% average success versus 26.67% for pi0.5. In long-horizon pour-over coffee preparation, a history-conditioned adapter raises post-failure completion at two filter-handling steps from 14% to 94% and from 8% to 82%, compared with A2-WLA retries. Our training infrastructure delivers 427.1 samples per second, 4.03x the throughput of a pi0.5 reference implementation on matched hardware. We will release the system, models, training scripts, and infrastructure to support efficient embodied learning.

title: SplatAnything: Gaussian Spacing Normalization for Feed-forward 3DGS across Arbitrary Scenes
abstract: We identify a key limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods: Gaussian attributes are typically predicted in a radial-distance-normalized space that canonicalizes a global radial statistic of the reconstructed geometry, while the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers can still vary substantially across scene scales and camera configurations. This mismatch induces systematic shifts in Gaussian-scale targets, leading to ambiguous supervision. To address this, we propose SplatAnything with Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm), which canonicalizes a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to provide a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction. To rigorously assess our method, we further establish a systematic benchmark spanning diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and challenging extrapolated viewpoints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SplatAnything achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains under substantial variations in scene scale and viewpoint.

title: Confucius4-R2T2: A Stable-Prefix Streaming ASR Model for Real Real-Time Transcription
abstract: Streaming speech recognition is increasingly consumed by machines, such as translators and voice agents, that act on each token as it appears. A token that is later revised costs wasted work or a wrong action. In this work, we present Confucius4-R2T2 (short for Real Real-Time Transcription), a stable-prefix streaming ASR model that never modifies its earlier output while maintaining high accuracy and low latency. R2T2 is obtained by post-training Qwen3-ASR-1.7B on 1,500 hours of Chinese and English audio while freezing its pre-trained audio encoder and projector. The adaptation is based on the concept of Longest Stable Prefix (LSP), a new notion that we introduce in this work. We prove that LSP is monotone under the prefix order, consistent with the full-audio output, and maximal among labels that equal a whole earlier output. Learning from LSP labels converts a full-context model into a stable-prefix streaming one without any architectural change. Extensive evaluations show that R2T2 brings streaming recognition close to the base model's full-context quality while delivering stable text with low emission lag. Its gains extend beyond the post-training languages, demonstrating a practical path from full-context ASR to stable streaming. We open-source the model weights and code at https://huggingface.co/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2 and https://github.com/netease-youdao/Confucius4-R2T2.

title: OneTrans-GSR: A Generative Slate Ranking Paradigm Unifying Reranking and Mix-Ranking with One Autoregressive Transformer
abstract: Industrial recommender systems allocate substantial computation to pointwise candidate scoring, yet separate reranking and mix-ranking stages still assemble the final exposure slate using hand-crafted rules and specialized low-capacity models. Mix-ranking combines product cards, short videos, livestreams, and advertising cards supplied by distinct upstream business channels. Although these rules and models encode valuable domain knowledge, they are inherently limited in leveraging additional data and computation. They constrain the combinatorial space of candidate slates and determine objective trade-offs through manual tuning. To enable scalable and effective slate generation, we reformulate reranking and mix-ranking as a unified learning problem whose performance can improve with computation. Specifically, we instantiate this formulation across the reranking and mix-ranking stages and propose OneTrans-GSR, a single decoder-only policy that extends our deployed OneTrans backbone to generate the exposure slate end-to-end. During training, a reward model evaluates complete slates and guides reinforcement learning toward slate-level and long-term objectives. During decoding, business constraints are explicitly enforced. Offline evaluation shows that slate quality consistently improves as reward-model and policy compute increase. Deployed in a large-scale industrial recommendation system, OneTrans-GSR mixes heterogeneous content types within a unified slate. In online A/B tests, it improves GMV/u by 2.63%, advertiser value by 2.06%, and repurchase rate by 2.03%, while reducing end-to-end latency across the reranking and mix-ranking stages by 13%. These results mark a paradigm shift in slate generation: moving beyond human-engineered heuristics toward a general learned policy creates a scalable path for further algorithmic optimization and compute-driven improvement.

title: P^2-MOPD: Accelerating Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation via Parameter Priors
abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation consolidates expert capabilities by supervising student-generated trajectories, whereas task arithmetic offers a training-free alternative through linear parameter combinations. We view the linear combination of student and expert parameters as a single differentiable model and propose P^2-MOPD, which jointly optimizes the mixing coefficients and the student weights under the same on-policy distillation objective. Unlike task arithmetic, which stays within the span of the frozen student and expert parameters for any choice of merging coefficients, P^2-MOPD keeps the student trainable, so the experts act as parameter priors without confining it to this span. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales, P^2-MOPD achieves faster and more balanced recovery than MOPD from the same initialization, surpassing its final average recovery in half the training steps. At the end of training, our 1.7B model reaches 94.7% average recovery, versus 80.9% for MOPD.

title: Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking
abstract: Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. To address this challenge, we propose Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine that decouples the logical tree structure of a decision request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. Through ForkAttention, Flide navigates request dependencies using GPU-resident indices across both standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, guaranteeing in exact arithmetic that every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass. By expressing branch topologies directly in GPU-resident metadata, Flide accommodates diverse request mixtures with a compact set of pre-recorded execution graphs while enabling expanding agent histories to resume from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. Extensive evaluations on public hybrid and decision models demonstrate that Flide answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance. By unifying physical execution throughput with mathematical exactness, Flide establishes a principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in agent systems.

title: Complaint from 2611.12799: forgetting across checkpoints is read from one greedy decode per checkpoint, with no noise floor
abstract: I call a problem 'forgotten' when one greedy decode of an earlier checkpoint got it right and one greedy decode of the best checkpoint got it wrong, and I never check whether a single checkpoint sampled twice would show the same churn: 'We use greedy decoding for all checkpoint evaluations' (sec. 2); my only robustness device is counting problems 'solved by at least $k$ of the checkpoints' with 'Raising $k$ drops the tasks only a single checkpoint ever solved' (sec. 2), and I concede that 'measuring how much of the historical task coverage can be reliably recovered' is still a 'useful next step' (sec. 5). No per-problem success probability, no repeated-decode noise floor and no confidence interval on the 2,808-vs-4,553 union gap are in the text; bootstrap CIs are mentioned only for SciWorld (App. A.2).

title: Complaint from 2611.12799: recovery is small, leaky, and measured on the selection set
abstract: My recovery is small, leaky, and measured on the set I select on: 'The student recovers 60 questions from the historical union while losing 45 previously solved questions, for a net gain of 15 questions (+0.75 percentage points, from 55.25% to 56.0%)' and 'substantial losses remain even at the best observed validation checkpoint' (sec. 4.3); 'Since this checkpoint is selected on the same validation set, the analysis describes consolidation behavior rather than independent test-set performance' (sec. 4.3); 'Recovery remains incomplete, however, and some tasks show regressions' (sec. 5), for example ALFWorld Heat falls from 96.0 to 92.0 (App. A.4). The test-set gain on the same backbone (+2.6 EM, Table 1) is three times the measured net recovery, so most of the gain is not accounted for by recovered coverage.

title: Complaint from 2611.12799: the consolidation stage is never priced or compute-matched against training longer
abstract: My stage costs extra rollouts and evaluations that I never price or match against simply training longer: 'filling the batch requires approximately $B / \rho$ sampled problems and $2BG / \rho$ rollouts, split evenly between the student and the activated teacher' plus a teacher forward pass per retained trajectory and 'evaluating the frozen teacher pool on the validation set and periodically re-evaluating the student' (App. A.3); 'Consolidation also requires additional sampling and evaluation, although deployment uses only the student. Reducing this cost ... [is a] useful next step' (sec. 5). No GPU-hour figure and no continued-GRPO or self-distillation arm at equal compute are in the text; the closest control, GTR-Turbo with additional RL updates, lands within 0.4 / 0.5 points on NQ / HotpotQA (Table 2).

title: Complaint from 2611.13254: one LLM annotator, no human agreement behind every fault-origin and evidence count
abstract: Every number in the trajectory-dependability study except the harness scan comes from one LLM annotator per trace and nobody has checked it: 'The records were produced by an LLM following a written protocol. We have no human inter-annotator agreement to report in this version' (sec. 5.1); 'A human check of a subset is the obvious next step, and we would not be surprised if it moved some of the kind labels, which were the hardest part of the protocol' (sec. 5.1). The only external check is that 'our origins agree with the human decisive steps within one step in 59% of cases' (sec. 5.1), and the two labels 'answer different questions' (sec. 3.4). The headline rates (origin at 0.18 of the run, 72% of failed runs with contradicting evidence, 88% of those unused, JUDGE reaching 74%) are therefore properties of protocol-plus-annotator until a human audit of a subset exists.

title: Complaint from 2611.13254: control-reach and restore-reach counts are trace readings, never run as interventions
abstract: The control-reach table (Table 4: independent judge 74%, task contract 67%, environment re-verification 43%, checkpoint 1%; restore sufficient in 35 of 95 runs) is a reading of the trace, not an experiment: '"Would have reached" is a judgment about the trace, constrained by the control contracts of Table 10. It is not a measured intervention. Whether a control would actually have prevented a given failure requires re-running the agents with the control in place, which we have not done' (sec. 5.1); the control table 'compares contracts, not measured efficacy' (Table 10 caption). The restore-reach count also presupposes the annotated origin is right. Nobody has re-run a failed Who&When or MAD trajectory with a judge that reads the unused evidence, or with a task contract fixed at admission, to see whether the counterfactual holds.

title: Complaint from 2611.13254: failure-only sandbox corpora with no external effects, a non-random sample, and a harness-fault scan run on one corpus only
abstract: The corpora cannot show the failures the framework was built for and the sample is neither random nor complete: 'Both corpora are question answering and programming in sandboxes. Not one run in our sample changes a shared or third-party system, so external impact (H5) and recovery of committed effects, which the framework was partly built for, cannot be studied here. That needs corpora like tau-bench or TheAgentCompany trajectories, or fault injection' (sec. 5.1); '96 annotated runs out of 203 normalized traces, selected by annotation batch rather than at random' and 'The MAD part is small and short-biased' (sec. 5.1). Every rate is conditioned on failure, so how often evidence is present and used in runs that succeed is unmeasured (App. D, Fig. 7: failure-conditioned corpora 'do not measure fault frequency'). The one annotator-independent result, that 26 of 58 hand-crafted Who&When runs (45%) end in a provider content-filter HTTP 400 with a harness-generated FINAL ANSWER (sec. 4.6), is 'a deterministic text scan over all 184 raw Who&When trajectories' (sec. 3.4) and has not been run on MAST-Data, LongRCA or TRAVERSE, the other corpora attribution models are trained and scored on; the paper only says 'Attribution benchmarks should mark such runs' (sec. 5).

title: Complaint from 2611.14068: variance decomposition attributes the within-episode share to the policy alone
abstract: My variance decomposition says 88.9% of the score is 'the policy's own sampling', but the within-episode component is 'the closed-loop response to the policy's draw, red and green included' (sec. 5), I never hold the policy's actions fixed and redraw the adversary, and my two defenders are not even reseeded the same way: 'the two harnesses reseed different generators with the policy seed, so the two defenders' sampling shares are not measured on the same footing' (sec. 10) — so I cannot say which party's draw moved the outcome, only that it was not the scenario.

title: Complaint from 2611.14068: the drop's cost is never measured on an agent that cannot see the busy flag
abstract: I measured the silent drop only where it does not bite: 'its cost on the policies themselves is measured by switching that check off (Section 6), an ablation of each wrapper and no measurement of an agent built without one ... we did not run an agent on the documented observation itself' (sec. 10), and the training-time cost of being rewarded and charged for directives the simulator never ran is 'a credit-assignment cost during training that we name and have not measured' (sec. 4.4).

title: Complaint from 2611.14068: the busy-check training effect is a package read from code, not separated
abstract: My training result is a package I cannot unpack: 'the mechanism is read from the code and not measured. A trainer that kept the check and credited the rewards earned while busy to the action that earned them, discounting per tick, would separate the credit assignment from the check itself, and that arm is future work' (sec. 6.4); it rests on four paired seeds (sign test $p = 0.125$) and three continuations, two of which are 'still moving when the budget stops it' (sec. 6.3), at 'days of CPU per seed' (App. A).

title: Complaint from 2611.15020: headline correlation with no uncertainty
abstract: My headline is one correlation with no error bars, and I say so myself: 'These describe task-specific Score differences, not success-rate differences or uncertainty intervals' (sec. II-E); 'Mini-plots show the final gap on a common -0.12 to +0.12 scale, not uncertainty intervals' (Table B1); 'There are no independent repeated real trials or uncertainty intervals in the supplied results' (App. C.3); 'repetition counts therefore do not support confidence intervals or population success rates' (App. D.5) [paraphrase: with 30-100 rollouts per pair, only 1 of 22 gaps is larger than its own sampling noise, operator computation].

title: Complaint from 2611.15020: physics layer never validated off its fitting data
abstract: My physics layer never validates on anything it did not fit on, and it does not reach the task Scores: 'The \"held-out\" time windows are later segments of the same recording; whole-trajectory feasibility gates and development inspection mean they are not blind independent tests' (sec. III-C); 'Each asset has one recorded real interaction' (sec. IV-B1); 'These robot-level evaluations do not establish an asset-linked benchmark benefit' (sec. IV-A); 'The current results do not establish a causal reduction in benchmark task-score discrepancy' (sec. IV-B3); 'Successful execution alone therefore cannot establish an identification benefit' (sec. IV-B3).

title: Complaint from 2611.15020: cross-engine contact rescued by hand-set damping
abstract: My cross-engine contact transfer is rescued by hand-set damping and stiffness with no force measurement to check against: 'Native simulated contact forces use different readback semantics, and no real contact-force reference is supplied' (sec. III-C); 'Strong damping is an effective engine adaptation rather than measured rolling friction' (App. D.2); 'The source path does not express MuJoCo solref/solimp equivalently ... Geometry, initialization, robot/observation calibration and numerical differences remain potential contributors' (App. D.3); 'It does not rule out other model and solver differences' (App. D.2); and the executable configurations are not archived: 'Exact limiter thresholds, coupling rules and filter recurrences/initial states ... still require executable configuration records' (App. C.3).

title: Complaint from 2611.16315: item-level floor measured under one narrow sampler, no thinking or long-budget run
abstract: My headline floor is measured under one narrow sampler and I cannot say how much of it is the sampler: all draws are at '$T = 0.4$ ... with top-$p = 0.95$, 1024 new tokens ... and thinking modes disabled' (Table 1); 'the temperature sweep covers four models (three of one family), one run and $T \leq 1$' (sec. 8); 'frontier, closed and reasoning models were not tested' and 'extended test-time reasoning, which our token budget excludes' is one of the 'two routes [that] remain untested' (sec. 8), so I do not know whether the item-level component survives thinking mode or a larger budget.

title: Complaint from 2611.16315: shared per-item errors have no identified cause; CONF and RATIONALE fields unused
abstract: My correlations say the models err together on the same items but not why: 'These are correlations of errors ... They do not identify the cause. Shared knowledge acquired from similar text, properties of the items and their construction, and errors in the answer key would all produce them' (sec. 4.1); my label audit flags 5.5% of items and 'most others are ill-posed' (App. C); 'SciOly's answer key offsets its signed errors, and Guesstimate has 15 items' (sec. 8); and I collected a CONF field and a factor-by-factor RATIONALE on every answer (App. A) that the analysis never uses to locate the shared error.

title: Complaint from 2611.16315: debate rounds parser-corrupted; intervention screen exploratory and prompt-mixed
abstract: My debate data are partly corrupted and my intervention screen is mostly exploratory: 'Rounds 2 and 3 were generated with a defective parser (Section 6); a definitive test of heterogeneous debate requires regenerating them'; 'the activation screen covers one model, 150 items and the median rule, and its model is recorded in the job configuration rather than in the stored results; $A$ is sensitive to winsorization when an arm inflates the spread'; 'Only the six prompt-level arms form a confirmatory family' (sec. 8), the plan 'was not registered publicly' (sec. 3.4), and 'the main sweep mixes two prompt pairs unevenly across models' so 'per-model levels of accuracy and bias, and their rank correlations, are prompt-dependent' (sec. 8).

title: Complaint from 2611.16526: delegation measured only on independent facts
abstract: My delegation study only ever asks for facts that do not depend on each other, so I cannot say what the orchestrator-executor boundary costs when one subagent's answer is the next subagent's input: 'we focus on small datasets of independent factual questions. Real-world tasks may consist of interdependent information needs. We deliberately study this simpler setting to test delegation without the additional challenges of task interdependence. Failures in these simpler settings raise concerns about generalizability to more complex settings' (2611.16526, sec. 7, Limitations).

title: Complaint from 2611.16526: orchestrator and executor always the same model
abstract: My orchestrator and my executor are always the same model, so a cheap executor under a strong orchestrator, the configuration people actually deploy, is unmeasured: 'we study configurations in which orchestrators and executors belong to the same model family. We do so to avoid a combinatorial explosion of heterogeneous setups. Studying the interplay between different model families is an interesting avenue for future work' (2611.16526, sec. 7, Limitations).

title: Complaint from 2611.16526: the return message's content and token cost never measured
abstract: I know the executor's return message loses the failures and the sources, but I never measured what it should carry or what that costs in tokens; I tried one prompt and ruled out the full-trace extreme by assumption: 'Instructing executors to report failures yields only limited improvements. Passing complete executor traces to the orchestrator could mitigate the loss of information, but would undermine the context-saving benefits of delegation' (2611.16526, sec. 7); 'Addressing this challenge may require targeted mechanisms for communicating evidence and resolving conflicts rather than simple prompt interventions' (sec. 6). No token count, brief or return length, or intermediate disclosure level between 'final answer only' and 'complete traces' appears in the text; the single-agent and delegated arms also differ in tool budget (Table 7) and executor instruction (Table 8).

title: Complaint from 2611.16661: static one-scalar KV/recurrent-state split from a workload mean
abstract: My cache split is one scalar per workload, fixed before the run, from the mean final-turn footprint of trajectories on an earlier checkpoint, and I know it is not the live demand: 'This balancing ratio may not be optimal in practice, since the workload-wide mean KV-cache footprint may not reflect the cache demand of the trajectories active at a given time. Optional local calibration can identify a better-performing nearby ratio.' (sec. 3.1.2); 'The selected ratio $\hat r$ stays fixed during inference serving.' (sec. 3.1.2). My best measured ratios were 0.5-1.5x my formula's and I never say what that gap costs in minutes; hierarchical caching and hybrid-model eviction are future work (sec. 6).

title: Complaint from 2611.16661: tail scheduler blind to remaining chain length, no oracle bound
abstract: My tail scheduler knows only how many turns a chain has completed, not how many remain, and the tail is now most of the batch: 'With future trajectory lengths unknown, CAAS uses completed inference turns as a proxy for potentially long trajectories' (sec. 4.2); 'Although CAAS reaches 95% completion later, it finishes the batch earlier.' (sec. 5.3); 'The final 25 tasks under Opt-CAAS average 27.9 and 15.6 turns ... compared with 10.1 and 7.9 under the baseline.' (sec. 5.4). I never compare against a hindsight-optimal order even though my replay harness holds every recorded duration, I never report the chain-length distribution, and I get 1.9-3.5% in replay.

title: Complaint from 2611.16661: replay of survivors with frozen tool durations; three-run means without spread
abstract: My controlled ablations replay only successful trajectories with frozen tool durations, while the live environments I am protecting slow down with concurrency and my live numbers are three-run means with no spread: 'only successful historical executions were collected; failed executions were excluded' and 'it does not evaluate semantic correctness or cover all failures and retries' (App. A.1); 'Stage dependencies and environment durations remain fixed' (sec. 5.1); 'MCP-Atlas tasks depend on external MCP services, which may degrade under high concurrency or encounter upstream rate limits such as HTTP 429 errors.' (App. A.2); 'Stochastic model sampling and environment variability cause trajectories and token counts to differ across live runs.' (sec. 5.4). Makespan under TTFT/TPOT SLOs is also open (sec. 6).

title: Complaint from 2611.17316: harness and language: step saving flips sign under OpenHands
abstract: My memory's step saving is a property of one harness and one language, and I have shown the sign can flip: 'Our main experiments use Python repositories in the mini-swe-agent harness, and post-training covers the three open-weight actor models. Other programming languages and larger actor models remain to be tested' (Limitations); under OpenHands the same memory on the same frozen 27B actor takes 38.6 steps against 33.8 without it, and the post-trained actor takes 45.9, at 1,647K raw tokens against 897K (Table 6), so I cannot tell a user of another harness whether the memory will save effort or cost it.

title: Complaint from 2611.17316: steps charged, tokens counted, neither is the cost paid
abstract: I charge steps and count tokens, but neither is the cost anyone pays: 'We measure effort by steps and cache-aware tokens and do not report wall-clock latency or energy use' (Limitations); the reward of eq. 4 is $W - n_i$ on success, so tokens never enter the training signal, my token numbers are 'cache-aware' and credit the prefix caching a short fixed memory enjoys, and my dollar figures are 'a deployment-free conversion and not an expense' (App. B), so the 'cost-internalizing' claim internalizes one proxy and reports two others.

title: Complaint from 2611.17316: one memory at one boundary; accumulation over longer histories undefined
abstract: I write one memory at one boundary from one trajectory and never say what happens at the second: 'How memory should be accumulated and refreshed over longer repository histories is future work' (Limitations); my template is per-task (FILES / STATUS / VERIFY / DID describe 'THIS session's task only', App. L), my chains are read one boundary at a time, and on SWEContextBench I had to rewrite the writer instruction 'after observing the first runs on the set, whose memories were getting cut off because of note length' (Table 5 caption), so a memory that must survive three or ten tasks on one repository has no design and no valuation here.

title: The return is the relay the lane modelled as lossless: trace the distortion-rate curve of the executor-to-orchestrator return (answer only, structured evidence, free summary, full trace) on frozen executor traces, with the orchestrator's accept / re-delegate decision as the relevant variable and its closed-book prior as decoder side information, and locate the knee that the information-bottleneck account of multi-agent systems assigns by hand
abstract: In information theory a lossy description is graded by its rate-distortion function: for a source $X$, a reconstruction $\hat X$ and a distortion $d$ chosen for the receiver, $R(D) = \min_{p(\hat x \mid x):\, \mathbb{E}[d(X,\hat X)] \le D} I(X;\hat X)$ is the fewest bits that reach distortion $D$, it is non-increasing and convex in $D$, and the information bottleneck turns it into the search for a short code of $X$ that keeps the information about a relevant variable $Y$, with the distortion emerging from the joint statistics of $X$ and $Y$ (Cover and Thomas ch. 13; Tishby, Pereira and Bialek 2000). The lane has imported the objective: 2607.16133 writes the worker-to-worker relay of a multi-agent system as an information bottleneck with a relay information loss $\mathcal{L}(R) = I(C;Y \mid S) - I(R;Y \mid S)$ and a per-task relay complexity $\kappa$, the minimum description length of a sufficient relay, assigned by task-structure analysis; 2606.13733 bounds success by a min-cut bottleneck; 2604.02460 argues from the data-processing inequality. What is not imported is the curve itself for the channel those papers leave uncompressed: the executor-to-orchestrator return. In 2607.16133 the aggregator receives the workers' terminal memories whole; in 2611.16526 (Lost in Delegation) the orchestrator receives the executor's final answer only, loses about 10 points on post-cutoff facts, re-delegates 6-9% of correct returns, and the authors write that full traces 'could mitigate the loss of information, but would undermine the context-saving benefits of delegation', a statement about a curve nobody traced. Carried into L4, that says: freeze each executor trace, serve the orchestrator the same trace at four rates (final answer; answer plus source URL, quoted snippet and tool-failure list, at most 80 tokens; the executor's free summary at 200 tokens; the full trace), and measure the orchestrator's item error $D(R)$ and its accept / re-delegate error against the oracle rule; the relevant variable is the orchestrator's decision, which depends on the trace through a few bits (did a source state the answer; did a tool fail), so the knee of the curve is predicted under 80 tokens and the answer-only loss is an operating point on the curve, not the boundary. Pre-registered: the structured 80-token return recovers at least 0.8 of the answer-only-to-full-trace gap on both open models (judgment 0.35); between 0.4 and 0.8 (0.30); under 0.4, the curve is gradual and no compact decision-sufficient statistic exists for this shape (0.35). The orchestrator's prior enters as decoder side information: items where the executor's answer contradicts the orchestrator's closed-book answer carry the excess error at low rate and the excess closes as evidence bits arrive. Position solo: World Bank and Nobel API ground truth, two open models the paper used, about 12 GPU-hours and $75 of search calls.

sentences: Rate-distortion theory answers 'what is the minimum rate description required to achieve a particular distortion?' (Cover and Thomas, ch. 13 introduction): the rate distortion function $R(D)$ is 'the infimum of rates $R$ such that $(R, D)$ is in the rate distortion region of the source for a given distortion $D$', and Theorem 13.2.1 says it 'is equal to the associated information rate distortion function' $R^{(I)}(D) = \min_{p(\hat x \mid x) \in F(D)} I(X;\hat X)$ with $F(D) = \{p(\hat x \mid x) : \mathbb{E}[d(X,\hat X)] \le D\}$, where $X$ is the source, $\hat X$ the reconstruction, $d$ the distortion and $I$ mutual information; $p(\hat x \mid x)$ is read as 'a hypothetical channel, a test channel, between $X$ and $\hat X$' (Purdue ECE Lecture 28).

The curve is 'a non-increasing convex function of $D$' (Lemma 13.4.1), so every description sits on or above it and the useful question about a description is where on the curve it operates, not whether it loses; and the distortion must be the receiver's, since for speech and images 'the mean squared error is not an appropriate measure of distortion as observed by a human observer' (sec. 13.2).

The information bottleneck defines 'the relevant information in a signal $x \in X$ as being the information that this signal provides about another signal $y \in Y$', formalizes the problem 'as that of finding a short code for $X$ that preserves the maximum information about $Y$', squeezing it 'through a bottleneck formed by a limited set of codewords $\tilde X$', and notes this 'can be seen as a generalization of rate distortion theory in which the distortion measure $d(x, \tilde x)$ emerges from the joint statistics of $X$ and $Y$' (Tishby, Pereira and Bialek, physics/0004057, abstract); a code is sufficient for $Y$ when $I(\tilde X;Y) = I(X;Y)$, which the lane's own import states as a relay information loss $\mathcal{L}(R) = I(C;Y \mid S) - I(R;Y \mid S) \ge 0$ that is zero for a sufficient relay (2607.16133, Def. 4.1), with $C$ the upstream context, $R$ the relay, $S$ the local subtask and $Y$ the downstream target.

import_sentence: In information theory a lossy description is graded by where it sits on the rate-distortion curve $R(D)$, with the distortion defined for the receiver and the information bottleneck telling the encoder to keep only what predicts the receiver's relevant variable $Y$; carried into L4, that says the executor's return to the orchestrator is a relay on such a curve (the one 2607.16133 modelled as lossless by handing the aggregator the workers' terminal memories, and 2611.16526 operated at one point, the final answer), its relevant variable is the orchestrator's accept / re-delegate / override decision rather than task success, the orchestrator's closed-book prior is decoder side information that is right pre-cutoff and wrong post-cutoff, and the curve's knee, traced on frozen executor traces at four return rates, is the quantitative relay complexity $\kappa$ that the information-bottleneck account assigns by hand and the number that says whether 'full traces would undermine the context-saving benefits' is a trade-off or a 50-token schema.

predicts.statement:
Setup: rebuild the forced-delegation arm of 2611.16526 on two open models it used (gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507, vLLM, temperature 1.0 as in the paper) with the two datasets whose ground truth is a public API, GDP (World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG, 30 four-country sets, 2019 and 2025) and Nobel (Nobel Prize API, 2014-2019 and 2025-2026), about 72 prompts and 310 items per split-pair, both pre- and post-cutoff, plus one web tool (SerpAPI search and a page opener). Stage 1 freezes the orchestrator's briefs $u_i$ per item $i$. Stage 2 runs the executor once per brief and stores the full trace $C_i$ (queries, snippets, opened pages, HTTP failures, final answer $a_i$) and a second trace for re-delegation. Stage 3 runs the orchestrator's integration step on the same frozen traces at four return rates: $M_i^{(0)} = a_i$ (final answer only, the paper's setting); $M_i^{(1)} = (a_i, 	ext{source URL}, 	ext{quoted snippet} \le 25 	ext{ words}, 	ext{tool-failure list})$, at most 80 tokens; $M_i^{(2)}$ the executor's own free summary at 200 tokens; $M_i^{(3)} = C_i$ (full trace). Quantities: $D(R) = \Pr[\hat y_i^{(R)} 
e y_i^\star]$, the orchestrator's item error at rate $R$ against API ground truth $y_i^\star$; $D_Z(R)$, the share of items whose decision $Z_i^{(R)} \in \{	ext{accept}, 	ext{re-delegate}, 	ext{override}\}$ differs from the oracle rule (accept iff $a_i = y_i^\star$), read from the tool calls, never from a judge; the gap $G = D(R_0) - D(R_3)$ and the recovered fraction $\phi(R) = [D(R_0) - D(R)] / G$; the knee $R^\star = \min\{R : \phi(R) \ge 0.8\}$ in tokens, which is 2607.16133's $\kappa$ for this channel, estimated rather than assigned. Decoder side information: $b_i$ is the orchestrator's closed-book answer (the paper's no-tool arm), and items are split by $a_i = b_i$ versus $a_i 
e b_i$. P1 (knee): $\phi(R_1) \ge 0.8$ on both models, so $R^\star \le 80$ tokens, under 2% of a median trace. P2 (side information): at $R_0$ the error on items with $a_i 
e b_i$ exceeds the error on $a_i = b_i$ items by at least 10 pp, carried by re-delegation and override of correct executor answers; at $R_1$ the excess is under 3 pp, because the snippet is the likelihood term the decision needs and the bare answer is a point estimate the orchestrator weighs against its prior. P3 (brief, the downward channel, secondary): with the executor and $R_3$ fixed, verbatim-item briefs raise post-cutoff executor accuracy by at least 5 pp over orchestrator-written briefs and move pre-cutoff accuracy by under 2 pp, since the orchestrator's additions are information pre-cutoff (Table 3 of the paper: 93% correct for GPT-5) and noise post-cutoff (6%). Reported alongside: tokens per arm, so the context saved at each rate is a number for the first time in this shape; $n = 3$ orchestrator draws per (prompt, rate) at temperature 1.0 and one at temperature 0; prompt-cluster bootstrap intervals.
predicts.expected: Judgment, not evidence: probability 0.35 that P1 holds ($\phi(R_1) \ge 0.8$ on both models); 0.30 that $\phi(R_1)$ lies in $[0.4, 0.8)$ (the knee is at the 200-token summary or the curve has no knee below the full trace); 0.35 that $\phi(R_1) < 0.4$ on at least one model (gradual curve). The paper's own one-field variant (an instruction to report inaccessible URLs: GPT-5 GDP post-cutoff $0.43 \to 0.51$ against a single-agent 0.89, GPT-OSS $0.70 \to 0.62$) recovered under a fifth of its gap with budgets and briefs unmatched, which is why P1 is not given more than 0.35. Probability 0.5 for P2, 0.5 for P3. Expected mechanism: the orchestrator decides accept or re-delegate by weighing a bare answer against its own belief; the trace content that would change that decision, whether a page stated the answer and whether a tool failed, is a few bits, cheap to send and absent at the answer-only operating point, so the loss is the rate, not the boundary.
predicts.field_assumes: Three stated positions. (i) 2611.16526 sec. 7: 'Passing complete executor traces to the orchestrator could mitigate the loss of information, but would undermine the context-saving benefits of delegation', and sec. 6: 'Addressing this challenge may require targeted mechanisms for communicating evidence and resolving conflicts rather than simple prompt interventions' - a trade-off asserted with no rate measured and tokens never counted. (ii) 2607.16133: the bounded relay is the worker-to-worker message; 'The system-level aggregator then combines all terminal memories into the final output' (sec. 3), so the upward return is uncompressed in the model; relay complexity is 'assigned by task-structure analysis rather than estimating it quantitatively' (sec. 7), and WideSearch-shaped parallel subqueries are placed in the low-$\kappa$ regime because 'no cross-worker relay is required' (sec. 5.2). (iii) 2604.02460 argues from the data-processing inequality that a message between agents can only lose information, with no curve. The field's own assumption is the opposite of (i): a description is graded by its position on $R(D)$, and the receiver's distortion decides what to keep.
predicts.belief_changing: If P1 holds, the 'delegation boundary' cost on fact lookups is an operating-point choice worth about 10 points and 50-80 tokens, every orchestrator harness that returns final answers (Claude Code subagents, OpenAI Agents SDK handoffs, Magentic-One's ledger, SearchSwarm's 'return results properly') has a schema to ship, MAS-versus-SAS papers report the return rate they operated at, and 2607.16133's $\kappa$ has an estimator. If $\phi(R_1) < 0.4$, the orchestrator's decision depends on diffuse trace content, no compact decision-sufficient statistic exists for this shape, the context-saving conflict is real, and the recipe is not to isolate contexts for lookups the orchestrator must adjudicate - a footnote 2607.16133 would cite as a high-$\kappa$ return channel on a task family they placed in the low-$\kappa$ regime. If $G < 2$ pp on both models with traces frozen, the paper's 10-point loss did not pass through the return channel (budget, prompt and brief confounds), which revises the card's reading of the result. If P2 holds, the post-cutoff loss is a side-information effect: the orchestrator's prior is a wrong decoder and the bits that fix it are evidence, not more answer.

identifiability: Random given: fixed prompt set, fixed frozen briefs $u_i$ and executor traces $C_i$ (stored once; every rate arm replays the same bytes, so tool budgets, page contents and HTTP failures are identical across arms by construction), fixed orchestrator model and prompt with only the return field changed, fixed return formatter $f_R$ (deterministic extraction for $R_1$: URL and snippet copied from the trace's opened page that contains the answer string, failures copied from HTTP status; the executor writes $R_2$ once and it is frozen). Whose temperature: the orchestrator's integration step samples at temperature 1.0 (the paper's setting), so $D(R)$ at that setting includes decision variance, reported with $n = 3$ draws and prompt-cluster bootstrap; a temperature-0 arm (one draw) reports the same curve without sampling variance, and the knee is required to agree within one rate level across the two arms or the result is reported as temperature-dependent. $D(R)$ is an error rate, defined at any temperature; it is not a variance and does not vanish at temperature 0. Whose property: the curve belongs to (orchestrator model, orchestrator prompt, return schema) on this item population; the knee is a property of the orchestrator's decision function and the task's information structure, not of the executor, whose output is frozen; the schema for $R_1$ is a protocol choice and is reported beside a second schema (the paper's 'report inaccessible URLs' instruction, executor-written) so that the knee is not an artifact of one field list. Post-cutoff status is per model (gpt-oss-120b cutoff 2024-06-01; Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 release 2025-07-31, 'the actual knowledge cutoff may therefore be earlier', 2611.16526 App. A), checked by the closed-book arm's accuracy under 0.06 as in the paper's Table 2. Judge versus verifier: item correctness is exact match against the World Bank and Nobel API values (GDP within 0.1 percentage points as in the paper), and the decision $Z$ is read from whether call_subagent was issued again and whether the final answer equals $a_i$; no LLM judge anywhere. The side-information split uses $b_i$ from the same model's no-tool arm, so 'contradicts the prior' is defined by the model's own closed-book output, not by an annotator.

probe.design: Step 1 (3 days, no GPU): rebuild GDP and Nobel prompt sets from the World Bank and Nobel Prize APIs following 2611.16526 sec. 3 and Table 6 (30 four-country sets x 2 years; laureates 2014-2019 and 2025-2026); write the forced-delegation harness with three stages (freeze briefs; run executors and store traces; replay returns to the orchestrator) and the four return formatters. Step 2 (about 6 GPU-hours, 1 day, $75 of SerpAPI): on 1 x H100 with vLLM, for each of the two models run the closed-book arm (for $b_i$), the brief stage, and two executor traces per item under orchestrator-written briefs and one under verbatim briefs, about 1,000 executor runs in total. Step 3 (about 4 GPU-hours, 1 day): orchestrator integration on frozen traces at the four rates, $n = 3$ draws at temperature 1.0 and one at temperature 0, for both models, about 2,500 short runs; the second $R_1$ schema as a fifth arm. Step 4 (2 days): $D(R)$, $D_Z(R)$, $\phi(R)$, $R^\star$ with prompt-cluster bootstrap; the side-information split; the brief arm; tokens per arm. Optional step 5 (about $300 API): the same replay on one closed model from the paper (GPT-5) to check that the knee is not an open-model property.
probe.dollars: about $40 at H100 spot rates plus about $75 of SerpAPI calls (about 2,500 searches); $300 more for the optional closed-model arm
probe.days: 8 days: 3 of harness and data work, 2 of runs, 2 of analysis, 1 for the brief arm
probe.kills_if: Dead as a claim if $\phi(R_1) < 0.4$ on both models under both $R_1$ schemas with the bootstrap interval's upper end under 0.6 (no compact decision-sufficient statistic; the curve is gradual and the context-saving conflict stands), or if $G = D(R_0) - D(R_3) < 2$ pp on both models with traces frozen (the return channel is not where the paper's loss went; the result is then a confound note on 2611.16526, cited but not ours to build on). Dead as a ruler if fewer than 80% of items have a closed-book accuracy under 0.06 post-cutoff on both models (the post-cutoff split is not post-cutoff for these models) or if the temperature-1.0 and temperature-0 knees differ by more than one rate level on both models (the knee is a sampling artifact).

papers.title: When Do Multi-Agent Systems Help? An Information Bottleneck Perspective
papers.trick: Model a multi-agent system as a chain of workers passing bounded relay messages, prove that with unbounded relays it reproduces a single agent, define relay information loss $\mathcal{L}(R) = I(C;Y \mid S) - I(R;Y \mid S)$ and show on five benchmarks and three model sizes that isolated contexts help when the relay a task needs is short and hurt when it is long, more so for stronger models.
papers.did_not_do: The upward channel is lossless in the model: 'The system-level aggregator then combines all terminal memories into the final output' (sec. 3), so the executor-to-orchestrator return that 2611.16526 operates at 'final answer only' is outside its bounded relays; relay complexity $\kappa$ is 'assigned by task-structure analysis rather than estimating it quantitatively' and $\beta$ is 'a qualitative capability parameter rather than a directly estimated quantity' (sec. 7); the only sufficiency test is a two-point ablation that hand-deletes fields (sec. 6, Table 4), not a rate sweep; parallel-subquery tasks (WideSearch) are placed in the low-$\kappa$ regime because 'no cross-worker relay is required' (sec. 5.2), which is the shape where Lost in Delegation finds the loss; no tool-mediated post-cutoff facts, no orchestrator decision variable, no decoder prior, and models are Qwen2.5-7B, GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3.5-27B-AWQ.

papers.title: Lost in Delegation: Studying the Effectiveness of Task Orchestration in Generative Search
papers.trick: Split a multi-fact web-search question into per-fact subagent calls with the same model and it answers no better, and worse on post-cutoff facts, because the brief adds wrong guesses and the return hides failures.
papers.did_not_do: One return operating point (the executor 'returns only its final answer', App. A) and one prompt variant (report inaccessible URLs: GPT-5 GDP post-cutoff 0.43 to 0.51, GPT-OSS 0.70 to 0.62, sec. 6); no rate sweep, no frozen traces (every arm re-runs the executor, so budget, 403s and brief differences move with the return), tool budgets unmatched (Table 7), tokens never counted, the upward loss inferred from accuracy after a 403 and from re-delegation rates rather than measured on the return (card 2611.16526, information_asymmetry), and the full-trace arm ruled out by assumption ('would undermine the context-saving benefits', sec. 7). Third: 2604.02460 (card neighbour, abstract fetched 2026-11-15) holds thinking tokens equal and argues from the data-processing inequality that inter-agent messages lose information, with no curve and no return channel. Fourth: 2606.13733 proves an exponential success bound in a min-cut bottleneck of the task's constraint graph, validated on SWE-bench submissions, no measurement of any message. Fifth: 2603.19677 GoAgent optimizes a conditional information bottleneck on inter-group messages as a method (17% fewer tokens), no curve reported. Sixth: 2607.22448 attributes fact omission to nine pipeline layers in air-gapped agents with 75,476 synthetic trials, orchestration by LangChain and ADK, no orchestrator decision and no rate sweep. Pre-window precedents with their tricks: IMAC 1911.06992 (information-bottleneck message compression for bandwidth-limited MARL communication) and CGIBNet 2112.10374 (graph information bottleneck under a bandwidth constraint).

nearest.verdict: The objective is made; the curve for this channel is not. 'Multi-agent design is fundamentally an information-bottleneck optimization problem' is in print (2607.16133, with 2606.13733, 2603.19677, 2604.02460 and the MARL precedents), so an import that said only 'orchestration messages are a bottleneck' would be already-made. What is filed is the field's next step for the return channel specifically: 2607.16133 hands the aggregator the workers' terminal memories whole and assigns $\kappa$ by hand; 2611.16526 operates the return at one point, re-runs the executor in every arm and never counts tokens; no fetched source freezes executor traces and traces $D(R)$ across return rates with the orchestrator's decision as the relevant variable or splits items by the orchestrator's prior. It is not a rename of the W42 S3xF5 record (compaction as one message to one's future self, graded against a Fano or communication-complexity bound that is vacuous for 1-bit outcomes, residual = best-of-N headroom): here the receiver is a different agent with its own prior and a discrete decision, the relevant variable is that decision rather than task success, the curve is estimated at four operating points on frozen traces with no bound and no best-of-N, and the channel is the one the lane's own import left uncompressed. It is not a rename of 2611.16526's return-handling rates (sec. 5.4), which are reactions to one operating point. Two-year density: 13 field-word and 82 lane-word hits, about one on-point orchestration-communication paper a month; race window about 3 months against an 8-day probe.

reason_for_pick: S10 is this week's live shape through the two new L4 cards (2611.16526: same-model delegation loses about 10 points post-cutoff with the upward return loss only inferred and tokens never counted; 2611.13254: evidence present in an agent's input and unused, a per-handoff disposition the lane wants to measure). F5 is in Jacob's evaluable set; its compaction import (S3xF5) was closed in W42 as already-made because the bound is vacuous and the residual is best-of-N headroom, so the question was whether the orchestrator-executor channel, two-way with a receiver who decides, is a different object. It is: the TAMU information-bottleneck account (2607.16133, read in full) bounds worker-to-worker relays and hands the aggregator whole memories, so the return channel Lost in Delegation operates at 'final answer only' is the unmeasured level, and the datasets with public-API ground truth make the probe a replay on frozen traces at about 12 GPU-hours.

scorecard.target_value: In print: 2611.16526 sec. 7 ('could mitigate the loss of information, but would undermine the context-saving benefits of delegation'; 'targeted mechanisms for communicating evidence'); 2607.16133 sec. 7 ('Future work should develop quantitative estimators for both'); 2611.17041 ('subagents must return reliable evidence'; a rubric on 'the research utility of each subagent report'); 2606.09730 ('constraining subagents to return results properly'); 2611.13254 sec. 4.2 (evidence 'in an agent's input and never mentioned'). Who pays: every harness that returns final answers from subagents; delegation-training teams whose rubric grades the return; MAS-versus-SAS authors whose comparisons sit at an unreported rate.

relevance.jacob_edge: Direct: rate-distortion, sufficiency and the information bottleneck are his to check and to say in a talk; the design is an identity-first measurement (freeze the source, vary the rate, read the receiver's error) with no learned component.

kill_probe.step: Steps 1-4: frozen executor traces on rebuilt GDP and Nobel sets, four return rates, two open models, $n = 3$ draws at temperature 1.0 and one at temperature 0; $D(R)$, $D_Z(R)$, $\phi(R)$, $R^\star$ with prompt-cluster bootstrap; side-information split by the closed-book answer.

scorecard.density_and_ownership: Occupied: the information-bottleneck objective for inter-agent relays (2607.16133, Jul 2026; 2603.19677 GoAgent's conditional IB as a method; 2606.13733's min-cut bound; 2604.02460's data-processing argument; IMAC 1911.06992 and CGIBNet 2112.10374 in MARL); the single-point measurement of the answer-only return (2611.16526, Nov 2026); per-layer omission attribution in pipelines (2607.22448); harness and benchmark pressure on 'return results properly' (SearchSwarm 2606.09730, ClawArena-Team 2606.31174); return-quality rubrics in training (LEAD-RL 2611.17041, this week). Unoccupied in every fetched source: a rate sweep of the executor-to-orchestrator return on frozen traces, the orchestrator's decision as the relevant variable, the knee as an estimated $\kappa$, the orchestrator's prior as decoder side information, and tokens counted per return. Natural first movers: the TAMU group (they own the formalism and list quantitative estimation as future work, for worker-to-worker relays), the Lost in Delegation authors (they own the datasets; release status unknown, which is why the probe rebuilds from public APIs), and the SearchSwarm / LEAD-RL groups (they own trained delegators). The re-open test is asking them. Race window: about one on-point paper a month in this sub-shape against an 8-day probe; proper-shaped from the solo position.
scorecard.why_now: 2607.16133 (2026-07-17) wrote the relay bottleneck and left the aggregator's input uncompressed and the relay complexity hand-assigned; 2611.16526 (2026-11-12) measured the answer-only return's cost in accuracy on datasets whose ground truth is a public API (World Bank, Nobel Prize), which makes a frozen-trace replay a one-week build; 2611.17041 (2026-11) and 2606.09730 (2026-06) made the subagent report a training target with a rubric and no schema; the two open models the paper used serve on one H100 under vLLM.
scorecard.register_and_what_it_is_not: Measurement register: a distortion-rate curve at four operating points on frozen traces, with a mechanism (the orchestrator's decision uses a few bits of the trace that the answer-only return discards; its prior is a wrong decoder post-cutoff) and a consequence each way (a return schema at the knee; or do not isolate contexts for adjudicated lookups). It is not a new orchestrator, not a relay-training method, not a bound, not a compaction result (the W42 S3xF5 record), and not a re-analysis of 2611.16526's judge-labelled return reactions.
